experiences.text: Flag feedback loops where retiring a type permanently removes it from known_types, making it impossible to re-evaluate or re-promote.
Call out when a feature's stated purpose (prevent LLM hallucination pollution) contradicts its default-off shipping posture, leaving production unprotected.
Prioritize identifying edge cases in statistical aggregation (like division by zero) and ensuring deterministic behavior independent of input order.
Flag dangerous footgun defaults where an empty-but-non-None parameter silently rejects all valid data.
Note when a source-specific behavior (e.g., only 'tfgrpo' eligible for retire) creates blind spots for other valid sources like 'counting'.
Avoid suggesting refactoring to reduce code duplication on functional changes.
Skip minor naming nits like cryptic test-literal shortcuts ('o/r') that do not affect correctness or maintainability.
Avoid speculative dependency concerns (e.g., PyYAML availability) unless a concrete breakage path exists.
Do not enumerate broad lists of untested edge cases; focus on the few gaps with real production correctness impact.

When two workflow files must share identical cache keys or version pins, flag the duplication as a silent-failure risk and propose a concrete single-source-of-truth mechanism (repo variable, composite action, or CI assertion).
When a cache restore uses an exact key only, recommend adding restore-keys with a prefix fallback so partial dependency changes don't force a full rebuild.
When an env var is set to the string "false" in YAML, verify the consuming code does an explicit boolean parse rather than a truthiness check on the non-empty string.
When a cache-warming workflow has no concurrency block, call out the race condition on save and propose a concurrency group.
When comments cite a future-dated policy as justification for an architectural change, ask the author to verify and link the official source before merging.
Do not raise concerns about third-party private-API usage that already exists in the codebase and is not introduced or modified by the PR under review.
Do not speculate about multi-OS or multi-arch cache matrices when the repo runs on a single platform—this is over-engineering noise the author will dismiss.
Do not raise speculative CI permission-scope failure modes (e.g., branch-protection 403) without evidence of an actual misconfiguration or failed run.
Avoid nitpicking single commented-out config lines as a standalone finding; fold minor comment-hygience notes into a more substantive review point or omit entirely.
Do not relabel the same cache-key duplication concern under generic finding types like PRA-MAINTENANCE or PRA-RACE when a more specific type (PRA-PREVENT) already covers it with stronger framing.
Prioritize identifying critical runtime errors such as division by zero in weighted average calculations.
Provide specific analysis of configuration changes, such as gitleaks allowlists, and propose concrete mitigations for potential false positives.
Call out untested production-failure paths for LLM consumers—malformed JSON, truncated output, and empty-candidate cascades are the highest priority.
Do not speculate about hardcoded threshold values needing configurability or significance testing unless the repo already uses such patterns.
Avoid deep hypothetical false-positive analysis on regex patterns without evidence of actual false positives in real data.
Ignore concerns about locked entries retaining non-canonical formats, as preserving manual overrides is an intentional feature.
Do not flag missing internal documentation cross-references or doc-section pointers as actionable issues.
Do not propose observability refactors (stderr to logging module) mid-feature unless the repo already uses structured logging.
Flag cross-document references that will 404 because they use repo-root-relative paths instead of sibling-relative links inside docs/.
Call out file:line citations that will rot on the first refactor and recommend stable symbol anchors or a pinned commit SHA.
Warn when the diff is truncated so critical downstream sections cannot be verified before merge.
Flag dates that are in the future relative to the merge timeline as likely typos that undermine provenance claims.
Highlight when a doc claims to have written back changes to another file but the PR diff does not include that edit.
Avoid deep accessibility nitpicks like missing aria-labels on emoji or table scope/caption requirements for internal design docs.
Do not report granular CSS issues such as undefined helper classes, fractional font-weight values, or one-off inline-style overrides.
Skip semantic quibbles about filename slugs versus in-body terminology when the meaning is clear from context.
Do not push abstract testability-philosophy concerns about acceptance-anchor measurability on design-doc PRs.
Refrain from asking open-ended clarifying questions that restate an already-flagged concrete defect.
Provide concrete parametrization recommendations (e.g., broken symlink) that are cross-platform-friendly and directly map to the fix's stated contract.
Use PRA-NIT (not PRA-INFO or PRA-RESOURCE-LEAK) for pre-existing minor issues in lines already being touched, keeping the finding proportional and actionable.
Omit praise findings entirely; they dilute the review and every review that included them scored the lowest reward.
Avoid deep exception-hierarchy analysis (e.g., UnicodeDecodeError is ValueError not OSError) that appears across all lowest-reward reviews and was not acted on.
Skip out-of-scope observations (non-mapping YAML, documentation suggestions, behavior asymmetry notes) that pad finding count without driving change.
Defer minor error-message improvements like appending a path string; they compete with core findings and reduce per-finding impact.
Dismiss suggestions to add string whitespace stripping for LLM content redundancy checks.
Avoid speculating about double-path-resolution bugs without first reading the callee implementation.
Skip speculative fallback-behavior concerns that existing tests already cover unless you can point to a concrete gap.
Suppress findings regarding low-level consistency issues like JSON encoding flags in test helpers.
Avoid repeating the same audit ask across multiple finding types in one review.
Do not speculate about hidden implementation details in truncated diffs—ask one focused confirmation question at most.
When a PR contradicts its own stated semantic principle (e.g., None vs 0.0), call out the specific contradiction concisely.
Do not enumerate hypothetical downstream null-handling failures without evidence of a concrete reader that will break.
Do not raise speculative default-parameter dangers unless you can name a specific call site that currently omits the argument.
Do not demand schema migrations or audits of all JSON consumers as a review blocker.
Never speculate about mock attribute completeness for attributes that may not exist in the real implementation.
Do not demand exhaustive caller audits when the diff is truncated—you cannot verify what you cannot see.
Only suggest missing test assertions when the existing test's intent is clearly violated, not when it simply does not lock every field.
Never report trailing whitespace or cosmetic nitpicks as standalone findings.
Do not split one underlying concern (null revert_rate) across multiple finding types and reviews.
Call out missing positive-control tests directly, not just the negative case, with a concrete mutation that would slip through.
When a defensive guard silently degrades to a value that re-introduces the exact bug being fixed, state that connection explicitly as a regression risk.
Flag when a fully-mocked integration test never exercises the real data-shape contract it claims to validate.
Identify verbatim-duplicated logic across modules and recommend a single canonical helper before drift occurs.
Demand a repo-wide grep for other instances of the same bug class before declaring the fix complete.
Do not restate verifiable facts as open questions; check the code and report the answer as a finding.
Avoid speculating about variable-name mismatches without first confirming the surrounding scope from the diff or repo.
Suggest referencing source code constants in tests instead of hardcoding strings to ensure synchronization.
Dismiss speculative security concerns about fallback text search mechanisms.
Dismiss naming nitpicks on internal helper functions if the current name is reasonably clear.
Ignore philosophical arguments about API abstractions when the functional contract is met.
Do not halt the review entirely due to a truncated implementation file; evaluate the provided tests and call sites.
Emphasize test coverage gaps that could cause silent regressions, such as missing boundary cases, untested set members, and absent combined-signal integration assertions.
Do not report explanatory comments as verbose if they clarify complex business logic.
Suppress documentation findings that focus on trivial formatting errors or typos without functional impact.
Frame defensive-code gaps as PRA-CONCERN with a concrete one-line fix suggestion rather than escalating to PRA-Bug or PRA-Risk for edge-case type issues.
Avoid cross-PR commentary about whether a sibling PR's precondition is merged yet; instead note the assumption inline as part of a PRA-CONCERN if needed.
Suppress test findings that question the structural validity of mocks or GraphQL payloads without pointing out a specific schema mismatch or test failure.

When a bootstrap path auto-promotes experiences, flag that evidence must capture the triggering metrics (fires, adoption_rate, agg snapshot) so operators can audit why a type was auto-activated without graduating.
When a new code path writes to a shared store, flag whether the caller assumes serial execution or needs explicit concurrency/locking documentation.
Do not flag monkeypatch try/finally cleanup as redundant—humans treat this as trivial style noise that obscures real findings.
Do not demand exact boundary-value test cases (fires=15 vs fires=14) as a HIGH-severity off-by-one risk; humans view this as over-specification of test coverage.
Do not flag test helper coupling or import-scope concerns for minor validation additions; these are below the threshold of actionable review feedback.
Flag concrete arithmetic or logic errors in test predicates and expected values with corrected code snippets.
Call out capsys/readouterr ordering issues that cause silent false-passes with a one-line fix.
Do not suggest replacing hardcoded test thresholds with named constants; reviewers treat this as noise.
Skip recommendations to import GRADUATE_MIN_SAMPLES or similar constants into tests; reviewers will not act on boundary-value philosophy.
Avoid speculative warnings about whether a monkeypatch target is reachable through module-local references.
Do not propose extracting rendered-string literals into shared constants just to reduce test-source duplication.
Suppress verbose capsys-buffering theory about reload/import ordering; keep only a one-line fix suggestion if at all.
Do not ask authors to annotate PR descriptions or CI expectations for step-dependency or red-green workflow.
Avoid broad requests to add end-to-end render-path coverage as a nice-to-have; reviewers deprioritize these.
Skip hypothetical concerns about future semantic changes to min_evidence counting that have no current failing symptom.
Do not write multi-paragraph warnings about importlib.reload global-state coupling; reviewers dismiss architectural test refactors.
Split compound assertions into separate lines to ensure test failures explicitly identify the incorrect field.
Identify the untested default/off code path as the critical production path that must be covered.
Replace hardcoded indentation constants in CommonMark rendering with dynamic calculation to prevent future regressions.
Warn when monkeypatches can silently become no-ops due to import-binding style and suggest verification assertions.
Disregard circular dependency warnings that originate solely from imports located within test files.
Do not critique docstring length or formatting when the content is technically accurate.
Skip requests to extract shared constants for test string literals unless there is demonstrated drift.
Skip theoretical env-mutation-mid-request concerns; they add noise without realistic failure scenarios.
Do not complain about truncated diffs; focus on what is visible.
Avoid speculating about None-normalization internals when a test already pins the expected output.
Use PRA-B for high-impact behavioral concerns that pair the problem with a concrete, actionable fix (e.g., separate counters, gating logic).
Use PRA-C to flag specific, named test-gap edge cases (e.g., type-in-both-arms, missing-vs-None key) so they are immediately actionable.
Use PRA-A for concise naming or API-clarity improvements scoped to a single symbol, not broad architectural opinions.
Suppress PRA-OK praise on backward-compatibility or test coverage; humans dismiss positive findings as noise that dilutes actionable signal.
Suppress vague PRA-CONCERN rephrasings of issues already covered by PRA-B; humans dismiss concern-only findings lacking a concrete remediation step.

Call out tests that reach into private internals (_shadow_hash, _SHADOW_HASH_SCALE, _exp_id) instead of asserting through public API, since these coupling issues receive high reward across multiple reviews.

Highlight when sibling functions in the same feature domain read configuration from different sources (explicit params vs env vars), creating silent inconsistency that breaks marker attribution guarantees.
Identify concrete untested interaction paths with specific repro scenarios (e.g., include_shadow=True with empty candidate pool, protected_types filter at render level), not vague coverage gaps.
Do not report diff truncation as a code finding; it is tooling noise that humans dismiss and it crowded out actionable feedback in the lowest-reward review.
Avoid hyper-specific float-boundary edge cases (near 0.0, near 1.0, exact epsilon comparisons) unless there is demonstrated evidence of an actual rounding or clamping bug.
Skip requests to test env-var unset defaults as standalone assertions; humans prefer testing the behavioral contract (include_shadow=False path) over the raw env default value.
Suggest extracting inline styles into named CSS classes with concrete class-name examples like `.section-tight`.
Point out hardcoded hex colors that bypass already-defined CSS variables and recommend switching to `var(--good)` etc.
Flag future-dated timestamps and ask the author to confirm the intended date.
Do not exhaustively list every line-number reference; mention the staleness risk once with a constructive anchor suggestion rather than enumerating all instances.
Do not flag diff truncation as a file-content defect; it is a display artifact the author cannot fix.
Do not flag minor Chinese wording choices like abbreviated phrases in internal design docs.
Do not flag mobile responsive table overflow on internal documentation HTML that is primarily read on desktop.
Dismiss findings regarding abbreviation inconsistencies in configuration variable naming.
Do not suggest extracting shared CSS files across the doc series unless the PR explicitly touches multiple docs.
Do not speculatively ask the author to verify that referenced sibling documents exist; only flag cross-references you can confirm are broken.
Mention inaccessible internal references only briefly; do not belabor traceability arguments that duplicate other findings.
Call out tests that pass for the wrong reason because a guard short-circuits before the intended code path is reached.
Note silent regressions where a default-value flip silently degrades behavior for existing deployments without any warning or changelog entry.
Do not flag trivial whitespace or lint nits that add no review value.
Use generic PRA-SUGGESTION for actionable doc improvements rather than fragmenting into specialized DOC_ subtypes that dilute signal.
Ask whether audit findings are tracked in follow-up issues when the PR ships documentation of defects without code fixes.
Flag genuinely non-standard values like arbitrary CSS font-weights as quick-win nits when they are easy to verify and fix.
Collapse stale-reference concerns into a single PRA-SUGGESTION instead of spawning bespoke finding types that repeat the same line-number feedback.
Merge unverifiable-citation feedback into a broader PRA-SUGGESTION about source credibility rather than creating a dedicated category.
Fold grep-verification suggestions into the same PRA-SUGGESTION about rotting references to avoid redundancy.
Avoid dedicated finding types for CSS-sharing suggestions; treat as a low-priority PRA-SUGGESTION at most.
Roll TOC and anchor suggestions into the same PRA-SUGGESTION about navigability instead of a standalone category.
Express gap-tracking requests as a PRA-QUESTION about follow-up issues rather than a separate finding type.
Do not raise tone or rhetoric as a review finding for audit documents; it is not actionable and humans dismiss it.
Avoid scope-expansion suggestions about listing all reviewed functions; reviewers find meta-coverage concerns low value.
Do not propose CI lint rules for standalone HTML docs unless the repo already has such infrastructure.
Do not raise findings about truncated diffs or request fuller context—this repo's maintainers dismiss incomplete-visibility complaints.
Do not raise hypothetical robustness concerns about non-string YAML values or future key leakage.
Refrain from challenging logic assumptions that implement the PR's stated fix.
Avoid raising speculative security or visibility-scope concerns about trace banner content.
Do not flag test-level monkeypatch cleanup concerns as blockers for this repo's PRs.
Call out missing inline imports that will cause the test to fail before any assertion runs.
Verify that referenced fixtures and helper functions are actually defined or imported in the visible context.
Suggest parameterizing boundary tests over multiple max_rounds values to strengthen off-by-one mutation guards.
Warn about coupling assertions to volatile Chinese reason strings or internal round+1 offset conventions.
Ignore comments regarding the sufficiency of default fallback rules that were not modified by the current PR.
Do not flag minor assertion redundancy between precondition checks—reviewers treat these as harmless belt-and-suspenders.
Suppress nitpicks regarding exception subclass specificity when the existing generic handling is functionally correct.
Identify timing-based concurrency assertions that will flake under CI load and suggest deterministic coordination primitives like threading.Barrier.
Flag shared mutable state passed to parallel workers and recommend deep-copying or documenting a read-only contract.
Verify thread pool executors are used as context managers to guarantee cleanup on unexpected exceptions.
Do not raise findings about truncated diffs or request full visibility — focus on what is reviewable.
Skip trivial import-style nitpicks that do not affect correctness or maintainability.
Do not insist that hardcoded worker-pool sizes be made configurable unless there is concrete evidence of deployment needs.
Suppress 'the sentinel is decorative' critiques on test-only PRs; ai_raw_count==0 is an acceptable proxy and adding mock/spy suggestions reads as scope creep.
When raising the env-var-cache concern, frame it as a single concrete question with one verifiable check, not a multi-option lecture.
Do not flag intentional default-value changes as breaking changes or request migration notes; maintainers expect consumers to track defaults via the changelog.
Do not request exact-boundary tests at threshold values unless the diff itself introduces boundary-prone logic.
Flag runtime-crash bugs like a missing return statement with a clear reproduction path and the exact exception.
Raise reference-identity or contract-mismatch concerns with a concrete assertion to verify the assumption.
Suggest low-cost durability improvements like keying comments to function names instead of rotting line numbers.
Do not flag lines that merely restate a default value for explicitness; it is pedantic and unhelpful.
Avoid meta-philosophical concerns about hand-copied fakes drifting from upstream unless a concrete sync mechanism is offered.
Avoid speculative cross-test breakage warnings without evidence that an existing path actually triggers the new fake.
Always cross-check the environment variable configuration table against the prose text to ensure all newly introduced parameters are explicitly documented.
Verify that default values listed in configuration tables match the inline descriptions to avoid misleading users.
Ensure all relative paths mentioned in the documentation accurately point to existing files to prevent user confusion.
Suppress findings regarding metadata dates or fragile line number references in documentation.
Avoid fixating on informal counting shorthands in the PR title when the underlying document contents are internally consistent.
Do not speculate about future CI trigger types that don't exist in the current workflow file.
Avoid hypothetical cross-platform concerns unless the CI matrix actually includes the platform in question.
Skip file-handle-leak complaints on test-helper code that runs once and exits.
Do not litigate absolute vs softened wording in inline design comments that are not user-facing.
Avoid theorizing about regex edge cases six abstraction layers deep from a simple hygiene gate.
Avoid recommending end-to-end rewrites of passing tests solely to prove semantics already covered by other test files.
Avoid spending review budget on complaints about truncated diffs; instead, specify which concrete implementation properties you need to see proven via tests.
Pair non-obvious behavioral guards with concrete actionable mitigations such as named env-var knobs or docstring-documented conventions rather than open-ended observations.
Trace the actual runtime coercion path when GHA secrets inject empty strings and flag the concrete crash (e.g., int('') → ValueError) rather than abstractly noting 'verify the consumer handles it'.
Quantify the operational blast radius of a configuration change—e.g., 'zero retries means a single transient 5xx kills the run'—with the run-data context already available.
Explicitly document the precedence rules between the new unified configuration and legacy path overrides to ensure smooth migration.
Do not critique the sourcing or traceability of empirical numbers in YAML comments—treat those as author's rationale, not a review-grade defect.
Do not suggest splitting a PR into smaller batches or adding observability combinations unless you can point to a specific attribution failure that already occurred.
Do not opine on whether YAML comments explain 'why' vs 'what' or suggest relocating rationale to ADRs.
Do not argue that implementation contracts belong in docstrings rather than workflow comments as a review finding.
Do not file meta-commentary about commented-out code being 'archaeological' or needing an issue tracker.
Suppress allegations of copy-paste errors in dictionary key lookups that are based purely on variable naming conventions without verifying the logic.
Do not flag monkeypatch effectiveness concerns or suggest adding reloads if the test suite already utilizes module reloading to handle global state.
Disregard nitpicks about the length or complexity of detect hints in configuration files.
Dismiss hallucinated warnings about incomplete HTML file content or closing tags.
Do not flag line number references in documentation as maintainability issues.
Ignore inconsistencies in path prefixes or metadata dates.
Suppress maintainability concerns regarding hardcoded line numbers.
Do not report cosmetic issues like future dates in metadata.
Avoid suggesting changes to strict string equality assertions in path tests or demanding tests for file-system path conflicts.
Disregard inline CSS blocks in documentation files as maintenance overhead.
Do not flag the use of line numbers in design documents as a brittleness risk.
Avoid suggesting conversion of HTML documentation to Markdown.
Suppress warnings regarding hardcoded line numbers in design documentation.
Ignore potential CSS duplication across design documentation files.
Do not raise issues about the robustness of internal documentation links.
Ignore minor metadata errors such as typos in dates within documentation.
Do not flag the presence of inline CSS styles in HTML documentation.
Identify logical conflicts between regex patterns and placeholder filtering rules within the described implementation.
Do not flag potential mismatches between environment variables and default arguments.
Suppress warnings regarding data integrity or primary key changes found exclusively in test files for wiring PRs.
Suppress critiques of file I/O dependencies if they are limited to test execution environments.
Focus on detecting cache key synchronization errors between main and warm-up workflows.
Ensure the pip cache key generation covers all necessary dependency files.
Do not flag general architectural complexity or dual-path logic as a defect.
Dismiss theoretical concerns about ABI compatibility across Python patch releases.
Verify that the implementation enforces an exact match on the configured bot_login string rather than a suffix match to prevent spoofing.
Confirm that the production logic strictly isolates trust checks to prevent untrusted users from waiving findings via checklist markers.
Dismiss descriptive observations of test mock updates that lack actionable insight or highlight specific errors.
Verify that normalization tests explicitly cover all relevant punctuation and separator variants like periods.
Do not flag missing data population logic in a metrics aggregation PR if the ingestion layer is handled externally.
Do not flag list order determinism as a reliability risk unless the code targets legacy Python versions.
Avoid flagging undefined constant errors when the constant is likely imported from existing utility modules not shown in the diff.
Verify that new features are opt-in by default to avoid unintended filtering.
Ensure CI configuration values align with infrastructure resource limits.
Ensure empty configuration values are handled gracefully to avoid runtime errors.
Do not flag brittle string assertions in tests as a high-priority issue.
Do not flag keyword-based filters unless they represent a fundamental logic error.
Do not flag logging in test files as a security risk.
Avoid suggesting loop consolidation or micro-optimizations for simple iterations unless performance is a bottleneck.
Identify tests that directly import private implementation details to increase brittleness.
Dismiss purely observational comments that explain code logic without proposing actionable improvements.
Do not report missing implementation code in PRs that are primarily for release notes or changelog updates.
Avoid critiquing the impact of features based on the erroneous assumption that release PRs must contain the full implementation diff.
Disregard feedback regarding the verbosity of changelog entries for security releases.
Ignore nitpicks about metadata details like future dates unless they break the build process.
Avoid flagging generic security risks without offering specific technical context or actionable solutions.
Do not flag hardcoded strings in test mocks as maintainability issues during security reviews.
Avoid requesting additional edge case tests for straightforward logic checks if the happy path is already verified.
Verify repository access permissions to ensure `gitleaks` can scan code from private forks.
Validate that the workflow enforces a failure when security checks are skipped.
Anchor allowlist regexes to start and end positions to prevent evasion via substring inclusion.
Ignore suggestions to optimize regex boundaries to maintain the intended high-recall false positive tolerance.
Retain the full git history fetch depth to ensure maximum coverage of potential leaks.
Verify all call sites are updated to match the new signatures of `render_report` and `orchestrator.post_results`.
Ensure the findings truncation mechanism renders a visible warning to alert users of incomplete results.
Check for circular dependencies resulting from the migration of rendering logic from `checklist.py` to `render.py`.
Disregard nitpicks regarding the categorization of technical details or the inclusion of ephemeral test counts in the changelog.
Verify that all referenced local files and paths exist within the repository to ensure documentation integrity.
Do not flag minor formatting preferences such as empty table headers unless they critically impact readability.
Avoid requesting rewrites of technical explanations based on complexity or density unless the meaning is ambiguous.
Verify that source code diffs include the actual implementation logic described in the changelog.
Ignore validation of release dates when critical code implementation is missing.
Flag incomplete diffs that lack implementation files for features described in documentation.
Verify that all example files referenced in documentation or changelogs are present in the repository.
Do not provide style or readability feedback on changelog entries when implementation code is missing.
Dismiss trivial errors like typos in release dates when the PR lacks necessary code changes.
Do not request removal of inline comments or review process annotations.
Dismiss performance findings related to module import locations.
Prioritize flagging runtime ImportError risks caused by importing new modules that are absent from the provided diff.
Dismiss requests to clarify PR description phrasing regarding historical code behavior when the implementation itself is missing.
Enforce file-specific style guidelines like the Minimalism Principle and advocate for Type Hints to improve Python code quality.
Avoid suggesting moving module-level constants to a central configuration file if they are currently self-contained.
Do not recommend replacing simple string return types with dataclasses or custom objects for warning logic.
Do not propose refactoring print statements to the logging module for simple scripts unless the project already uses it.
Ensure shell scripts handle command failures explicitly to prevent exiting before custom error logic executes.
Clarify authentication requirements for accessing releases in external or private repositories.
Validate interpolated variables in command-line arguments to prevent injection vulnerabilities.
Do not report dependencies on tools pre-installed in standard GitHub Actions runner images.
Ignore warnings about breaking changes when the PR explicitly introduces the new functionality.
Do not flag missing implementation code in PRs that primarily update version numbers and changelog documentation.
Ensure version numbers increment sequentially according to semantic versioning standards without skipping initial patch versions.
Ignore hardcoded dates or placeholders in changelog entries and do not flag them as review issues.
Do not report potential type coercion issues for environment variables unless the implementation explicitly fails to handle empty strings.
Avoid flagging theoretical edge cases in logic functions that are already verified by existing unit tests.
Suppress warnings about the existence of persistence files unless the workflow definition explicitly lacks error handling.
Do not suggest adding integration tests for niche scenarios like file corruption unless core functionality is at risk.
Ensure boolean flags validate for the string 'true' explicitly rather than relying on variable truthiness.
Do not flag the definition of default constants in CI workflows as an architectural violation.
Suppress subjective critiques of default reward weights unless they represent a clear functional bug.
Do not raise backward compatibility warnings for internal metrics extensions unless existing consumers are explicitly broken.
Do not request docstrings or design documentation updates if inline comments sufficiently explain the new logic.
Dismiss language-based comment style violations to focus on functional logic correctness.
Prioritize reviews that identify undefined variable handling risks in workflow conditional logic.
Verify that job permissions are correctly updated when inlining steps from separate jobs.
Dismiss generic warnings about cache dependency paths unless specific file structure complexity exists.
Ignore nitpicks regarding typos or dates in inline comments.
Do not flag coupling to private methods in test assertions for ground-truth data collection features.
Ignore minor code redundancy in test mock setup functions.
Do not report the presence of unnormalized types for locked entries as a consistency error if the spec requires preserving existing data.
Suppress concerns about testing private interfaces when such tests validate complex normalization rules.
Dismiss theoretical atomicity gaps between closing and creating pull requests in bot workflows.
Ignore alerts regarding potential GitHub API eventual consistency delays in freshness checks.
Suppress suggestions to add JSON format validation when file path filters are already in use.
Do not recommend additional checks for branch existence in workflow_run triggered jobs.
Avoid flagging force-push risks on bot-specific branches in documentation or code review.
Stop flagging potential force-push failures in internal automation scripts.
Avoid flagging hardcoded branch names in tightly coupled CI workflows.
Ignore theoretical security risks regarding static JSON data files in trusted workflows.
Suppress warnings about repository administrative settings in code reviews.
Move imports performed inside functions to the module level for consistency and PEP8 compliance.
Avoid mocking or testing private implementation details to prevent brittleness during refactoring.
Dismiss suggestions to add test coverage for syntax errors unrelated to the current resource management refactoring.
Dismiss requests to add error handling for file existence when the PR strictly focuses on context manager usage.
Suppress suggestions to add strict type checking for JSON content outside the scope of resource management improvements.
Ignore demands for cross-file error handling consistency that do not pertain to the modified code paths.
Prioritize verifying that the implementation catches specific exceptions like ValueError during config parsing to ensure pipeline stability.
Verify that randomization logic for result files is implemented at the basename level to prevent conflicts in shared environments.
Confirm that directory cleanup logic utilizes recursive deletion methods to handle non-empty temporary directories generated by external tools.
Validate that the system triggers the intended fallback mechanism instead of crashing when encountering malformed configuration parameters.
Dismiss concerns regarding fragile regex patterns in tests if the current implementation reliably extracts the necessary data for assertions.
Ignore meta-commentary about test implementation details as long as the test assertions correctly validate the production code's error handling.
Overlook minor stylistic ambiguities in changelog entries provided the technical change described is accurate.
